content: 1. Due to incomplete information regarding the metabolism of eluxadoline, exercise caution when co-administering it with strong CYP1A2 inhibitors. Ciprofloxacin can increase erlotinib levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP1A2 metabolism. If severe adverse effects occur, consider reducing the erlotinib dose. 2. Ciprofloxacin and erythromycin base both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with drugs known to prolong the QT interval may increase the risk of torsades de pointes in predisposed patients, though this risk is lower with ciprofloxacin compared to other quinolones. 3. Ciprofloxacin and erythromycin ethylsuccinate both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration with QT-prolonging drugs may increase the risk of torsades de pointes in predisposed patients, though ciprofloxacin poses a lower risk than other quinolones. 4. Ciprofloxacin and erythromycin lactobionate both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration with QT-prolonging drugs may increase the risk of torsades de pointes in predisposed patients, though ciprofloxacin poses a lower risk than other quinolones. 5. Ciprofloxacin and erythromycin stearate both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration with QT-prolonging drugs may increase the risk of torsades de pointes in predisposed patients, though ciprofloxacin poses a lower risk than other quinolones. 6. Escitalopram increases the toxicity of ciprofloxacin by prolonging the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 7. Ciprofloxacin decreases the levels or effects of estradiol by altering intestinal flora. This applies only to oral forms of the hormone. There is a low risk of contraceptive failure, but caution and monitoring are advised. 8. Ciprofloxacin decreases the levels or effects of conjugated synthetic estrogens by altering intestinal flora. This applies only to oral forms of the hormone. There is a low risk of contraceptive failure, but caution and monitoring are advised. 9. Ciprofloxacin decreases the levels or effects of estropipate by altering intestinal flora. This applies only to oral forms of the hormone. There is a low risk of contraceptive failure, but caution and monitoring are advised. 10. Ciprofloxacin decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by altering intestinal flora. This applies only to oral forms of the hormone. There is a low risk of contraceptive failure, but caution and monitoring are advised. 11. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with etodolac may increase the risk of central nervous system (CNS) stimulation and seizures, particularly at high doses of fluoroquinolones. The mechanism is unknown. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 12. Ciprofloxacin and etrasimod may both increase each other's effects by prolonging the QTc interval. When initiating etrasimod, transient decreases in heart rate and atrioventricular (AV) conduction delays may occur. Co-administration with QT-prolonging drugs, including Class Ia or Class III antiarrhythmics, may increase the risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 13. Ciprofloxacin and ezogabine may increase each other's toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval. Slight and transient QT prolongation has been observed with ezogabine, particularly at doses titrated to 1200 mg/day. QT interval monitoring is recommended when ezogabine is prescribed with agents known to prolong the QT interval. 14. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with fenoprofen may increase the risk of CNS stimulation and seizures, particularly at high doses of fluoroquinolones. The mechanism is unknown. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 15. Ferric citrate decreases ciprofloxacin levels by drug binding in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Ciprofloxacin should be taken at least 2 hours before or after ferric citrate. Caution and monitoring are advised. 16. Ferric maltol decreases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Ciprofloxacin should be taken at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after ferric maltol. Alternatives should be used if available. 17. Ferrous fumarate decreases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Ciprofloxacin should be taken at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after ferrous fumarate. Alternatives should be used if available. 18. Ferrous gluconate decreases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Ciprofloxacin should be taken at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after ferrous gluconate. Alternatives should be used if available. 19. Ferrous sulfate decreases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Ciprofloxacin should be taken at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after ferrous sulfate. Alternatives should be used if available. 20. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of finerenone by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Serum potassium should be monitored during initiation and dosage adjustment of either finerenone or weak CYP3A4 inhibitors. Adjust finerenone dosage as needed. 21. Ciprofloxacin and fingolimod both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 22. Ciprofloxacin and flecainide both prolong the QTc interval. Ciprofloxacin has minimal effects on the QT interval, but caution is advised when used with other QT-prolonging drugs or in patients with additional risk factors. 23. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with fludrocortisone may increase the risk of tendon rupture due to the combined effects of quinolone antibiotics and corticosteroids. Use caution and monitor closely. 24. Ciprofloxacin and fluoxetine both prolong the QTc interval. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 25. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with flurbiprofen may increase the risk of CNS stimulation and seizures, particularly at high doses of fluoroquinolones. The mechanism is unknown. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 26. Fostamatinib increases ciprofloxacin levels by affecting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Monitor for toxicities of P-gp substrate drugs, and dosage reduction may be required when given concurrently with fostamatinib. 27. Ciprofloxacin and fostemsavir both prolong the QTc interval. QT prolongation has been reported with higher-than-recommended doses of fostemsavir. Use caution and monitor closely. 28. Ciprofloxacin and gemtuzumab both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 29. Ciprofloxacin and gepirone both prolong the QTc interval. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 30. Ciprofloxacin and gilteritinib both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 31. Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir increases ciprofloxacin levels by affecting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor closely. 32. Ciprofloxacin increases the effects of glimepiride, glipizide, and glyburide by pharmacodynamic synergism. Hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia have been reported in patients treated concomitantly with quinolones and antidiabetic agents. Careful monitoring of blood glucose is recommended. 33. Goserelin increases the toxicity of ciprofloxacin by prolonging the QTc interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes. Use caution and monitor closely. 34. Ciprofloxacin and granisetron both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 35. Ciprofloxacin and haloperidol both prolong the QTc interval. Ciprofloxacin has minimal effects on the QT interval, but caution is advised when used with other QT-prolonging drugs or in patients with additional risk factors. 36. Histrelin increases the toxicity of ciprofloxacin by prolonging the QTc interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes. Use caution and monitor closely. 37. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with hydrocortisone may increase the risk of tendon rupture due to the combined effects of quinolone antibiotics and corticosteroids. Use caution and monitor closely. 38. Ciprofloxacin and hydroxyzine both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 39. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with ibuprofen may increase the risk of CNS stimulation and seizures, particularly at high doses of fluoroquinolones. The mechanism is unknown. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 40. Ciprofloxacin and ibutilide both prolong the QTc interval. Ciprofloxacin has minimal effects on the QT interval, but caution is advised when used with other QT-prolonging drugs or in patients with additional risk factors. 41. Ciprofloxacin decreases the levels or effects of ifosfamide by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely, as CYP3A4 inhibitors may reduce ifosfamide metabolism and therapeutic effects. 42. Ciprofloxacin and iloperidone both prolong the QTc interval. Ciprofloxacin has minimal effects on the QT interval, but caution is advised when used with other QT-prolonging drugs or in patients with additional risk factors. 43. Ciprofloxacin and indacaterol both prolong the QTc interval. Drugs known to prolong the QTc interval may increase the risk of ventricular arrhythmias. Use caution and monitor closely. 44. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with indomethacin may increase the risk of CNS stimulation and seizures, particularly at high doses of fluoroquinolones. The mechanism is unknown. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 45. Ciprofloxacin increases the effects of insulin aspart, insulin lispro, and regular human insulin by pharmacodynamic synergism. Hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia have been reported in patients treated concomitantly with quinolones and antidiabetic agents. Careful monitoring of blood glucose is recommended. 46. Iron dextran complex decreases ciprofloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Ciprofloxacin should be taken at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after iron dextran. Alternatives should be used if available. 47. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of isavuconazonium sulfate by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 48. Istradefylline increases ciprofloxacin levels by affecting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Consider dose reduction of sensitive P-gp substrates. Use caution and monitor closely. 49. Ciprofloxacin and itraconazole both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 50. Ivacaftor increases ciprofloxacin levels by affecting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Ciprofloxacin increases ivacaftor levels by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor closely when co-administered with weak CYP3A4 inhibitors. 51. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of ivosidenib by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors may increase ivosidenib plasma concentrations, raising the risk of QTc prolongation. Monitor for increased QTc interval risk. 52. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with ketoprofen may increase the risk of CNS stimulation and seizures, particularly at high doses of fluoroquinolones. The mechanism is unknown. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 53. Co-administration of ciprofloxacin with ketorolac may increase the risk of CNS stimulation and seizures, particularly at high doses of fluoroquinolones. The mechanism is unknown. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 54. Lanthanum carbonate decreases ciprofloxacin levels by cation binding in the GI tract. Oral quinolone antibiotics should be administered at least 1 hour before or 4 hours after lanthanum. This interaction applies only to oral quinolones. 55. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of lemborexant by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. A lower nightly dose of lemborexant is recommended when co-administered with weak CYP3A4 inhibitors. Refer to the drug monograph for specific dosage modifications. 56. Ciprofloxacin and lenvatinib both prolong the QTc interval. Lenvatinib prescribing information recommends close ECG monitoring when co-administered with QT-prolonging drugs. 57. Leuprolide increases the toxicity of ciprofloxacin by prolonging the QTc interval, increasing the risk of torsades de pointes. Use caution and monitor closely. 58. Ciprofloxacin decreases the levels or effects of levonorgestrel/ethinylestradiol/ferrous bisglycinate by altering intestinal flora. This applies only to oral forms of the hormone. There is a low risk of contraceptive failure, but caution and monitoring are advised. Antibiotics may decrease hormonal contraceptive efficacy. 59. Ciprofloxacin increases the levels or effects of lidocaine by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP1A2 metabolism. Elevated lidocaine plasma levels may increase the risk of toxicity. Use caution and monitor closely.
